Field surveys conducted across the Cumberland Plateau region indicate that the Sooty darter (Etheostoma olivaceum) attains a maximum total length of approximately 8 cm [Li = approximately 8 cm], a modest size that is consistent with other members of the subgenus Oligocephalus. Gravid females collected during the early spring spawning period were found to deposit eggs with an average diameter of 2 mm, and from these measurements the wet weight at birth can be estimated at 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams]. This minute neonatal mass, characteristic of many darter species, reflects the substantial yolk reserves contained within the relatively large, demersal eggs that undergo external fertilisation after being deposited in the interstitial spaces of gravel riffles. The larvae that emerge following eclosion are endotrophic and remain dependent on their yolk sacs for several days before the onset of exogenous feeding, a trophic switch that marks a critical transition in early life history.

Analysis of length-frequency data from routine monitoring programs suggests that the total length at puberty for the Sooty darter is approximately 4.2 cm [Lp = approximately 4.2 cm], a size typically reached during the second growing season. This threshold corresponds to the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, after which males develop the intense blue-green nuptial coloration characteristic of the breeding period. Females of comparable size begin vitellogenesis and are capable of producing their first clutch, although the precise age at first reproduction may vary with local stream temperature and food availability. Individuals that attain this length threshold earlier in the season benefit from a prolonged spawning window, which can enhance their lifetime reproductive success. The relationship between body size and reproductive maturity in this species appears to be tightly constrained by the need to allocate sufficient resources to both somatic growth and gamete production.

The ultimate wet weight of adult Sooty darters has been estimated at 3.51 grams [Wwi = 3.51 grams] for individuals that have reached asymptotic body size, a value derived from length-weight regressions fitted to a large sample of field-caught specimens. This modest adult mass, typical of small benthic stream fishes, imposes significant constraints on fecundity, as gravid females can accommodate only a limited number of developing oocytes within their abdominal cavity. The allometric relationship between length and weight in this species conforms closely to the general pattern observed across the genus Etheostoma, with larger individuals exhibiting a slightly steeper mass increase relative to length than predicted by isometric scaling. Adult body condition fluctuates seasonally, with peak masses recorded immediately prior to the spawning period and lowest values observed during the late summer months when metabolic demands are elevated and prey availability may decline. These patterns underscore the importance of understanding energy reserves in the context of reproductive investment.

Longitudinal studies of marked individuals in a second-order tributary of the Caney Fork River have documented that the maximum lifespan of the Sooty darter is approximately 2 years [am = approximately 2 years] under natural thermal regimes averaging 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This relatively short lifespan, characteristic of many small, fast-living stream fishes, means that the species is effectively semelparous at the population level, with most adults dying shortly after their first and only spawning season. The timing of senescence appears to be linked to the energetic exhaustion associated with reproductive effort, as post-spawning adults exhibit declining body condition and increased susceptibility to predation and parasitism. Environmental temperatures play a critical role in modulating the pace of life history, with individuals inhabiting cooler headwater reaches occasionally surviving into a third year, while those in warmer downstream sections typically complete their life cycle within a single annual cohort. The thermal regime of 18 °C [T = 18 °C] represents an intermediate condition that balances growth rate against metabolic maintenance costs.

Habitat selection by the Sooty darter is strongly influenced by substrate composition and water depth, with adult individuals showing a marked preference for shallow riffles characterized by clean cobble and gravel deposits where interstitial spaces provide both foraging opportunities and refuge from piscivorous predators. Comparative observations with the closely related Etheostoma blennioides suggest that the Sooty darter occupies a narrower thermal niche, rarely being collected from streams where summer water temperatures exceed 24 °C for prolonged periods. Diet analyses reveal a reliance on benthic macroinvertebrates, with chironomid larvae and ephemeropteran nymphs constituting the bulk of ingested prey items across all size classes. The species exhibits a diurnal foraging pattern, with peak feeding activity observed during mid-morning and late afternoon when light levels are sufficient for visual prey detection. These ecological attributes, combined with the life history parameters described above, position the Sooty darter as a representative member of the diverse riffle-dwelling darter assemblage characteristic of the Cumberland River drainage.
